---
title: "Evaluating models"
subtitle: "Read a score only after asking what it was compared with"
description: "Learn why model evaluation needs a baseline, repeated splits, and a split scheme that matches the claim."
categories: [model development, evaluation, text classification]
---

A program manager sees a model accuracy of 61 percent. She asks how an
always-majority prediction would compare.

The model's accuracy does not establish useful performance if a simpler rule
achieves the same result.

This lesson reads a committed split study for three related text models. The era
model performs better than simple alternatives. The party model, with these
features and this fixed penalty, does not consistently predict party correctly.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- separate candidate selection, the final test, and robustness checks.
- compare every score with a deployable largest-class baseline.
- read the spread across repeated train/test splits.
- explain what paragraph, speech, and person splits measure.
- use a confusion matrix and balanced accuracy.
- say when a specific model did not learn the target.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Start with the baseline

A **baseline** is a simple rule against which the team evaluates a model. The
largest-class baseline always predicts the most common training label. Its
simplicity makes it a useful comparison. A model that cannot improve on that
rule does not demonstrate useful performance.

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(tibble)
  library(stringr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(rsample)
  library(recipes)
  library(textrecipes)
  library(parsnip)
  library(workflows)
  library(yardstick)
  library(broom)
  library(glmnet)
})

study <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/split-study.csv",
  na = c("", "NA"),
  col_types = cols(
    task = col_character(),
    split_scheme = col_character(),
    replicate = col_integer(),
    accuracy = col_double(),
    bal_accuracy = col_double(),
    train_majority_accuracy = col_double(),
    test_majority_rate = col_double(),
    length_rule_accuracy = col_double(),
    test_rows = col_integer(),
    test_speeches = col_integer()
  )
)

baselines <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/baselines.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    task = col_character(),
    outcome = col_character(),
    rows = col_integer(),
    speeches = col_integer(),
    people = col_integer(),
    largest_class = col_character(),
    baseline_accuracy = col_double()
  )
)

split_levels <- c("paragraph", "speech", "president")
task_levels <- c("era", "era_party_rows", "party")

task_labels <- c(
  era = "era",
  era_party_rows = "era on party rows",
  party = "party"
)

split_summary <- study |>
  mutate(
    task = factor(task, levels = task_levels),
    split_scheme = factor(split_scheme, levels = split_levels)
  ) |>
  group_by(task, split_scheme) |>
  summarise(
    replicates = n(),
    mean_accuracy = mean(accuracy),
    mean_bal_accuracy = mean(bal_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    bal_accuracy_missing = sum(is.na(bal_accuracy)),
    mean_train_majority = mean(train_majority_accuracy),
    mean_test_majority = mean(test_majority_rate),
    mean_length_rule = mean(length_rule_accuracy),
    low_accuracy = min(accuracy),
    high_accuracy = max(accuracy),
    low_train_majority = min(train_majority_accuracy),
    high_train_majority = max(train_majority_accuracy),
    low_length_rule = min(length_rule_accuracy),
    high_length_rule = max(length_rule_accuracy),
    mean_test_speeches = mean(test_speeches),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(task, split_scheme)

baseline_display <- baselines |>
  mutate(task = factor(task, levels = task_levels)) |>
  arrange(task) |>
  transmute(
    task = recode(as.character(task), !!!task_labels),
    rows,
    speeches,
    people,
    largest_class,
    baseline_accuracy
  )
```

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  baseline_display |>
    mutate(baseline_accuracy = round(baseline_accuracy, 4)),
  col.names = c("Task", "Rows", "Speeches", "People", "Largest class", "Corpus baseline"),
  caption = "Corpus-level baselines and task sizes",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(study), 90L),
  identical(nrow(baselines), 3L),
  identical(sort(unique(study$replicate)), 1:10),
  all(split_summary$replicates == 10L),
  identical(round(baseline_display$baseline_accuracy, 4), c(0.6478, 0.7452, 0.6065)),
  identical(baseline_display$people, c(40L, 31L, 31L)),
  identical(baseline_display$speeches, c(60L, 47L, 47L)),
```

The era task has `r baseline_display$rows[baseline_display$task == "era"]` rows,
`r baseline_display$speeches[baseline_display$task == "era"]` speeches, and
`r baseline_display$people[baseline_display$task == "era"]` people. The party
model can train only on rows with a Democratic or Republican label, so it uses
`r baseline_display$rows[baseline_display$task == "party"]` rows from
`r baseline_display$speeches[baseline_display$task == "party"]` speeches by
`r baseline_display$people[baseline_display$task == "party"]` people. The
remaining rows come from other party labels. Each task also selects its own 500
tokens from its own training data.

## Selection, the final test, and robustness do different jobs

Lesson 43 compared candidate settings with five grouped folds from the training
speeches. After fixing the candidate and penalty, it used the 14 untouched test
speeches once. That final test evaluates the modeling decision within this
worked example. Transfer to another collection requires evaluation on a new
corpus.

The study below creates new splits 10 times to show how scores vary with the
allocation of speeches. These holdouts provide a **robustness check** on
sensitivity to the split. They are not 10 new untouched test
sets. Lesson 43 did not use them to choose its candidate.

**Accuracy** is the share of rows with the right label. When classes are uneven,
a model can get many rows right by favoring the larger class. A **confusion
matrix** shows which labels were confused, and **balanced accuracy** averages the
accuracy within each class so the smaller class still counts.

## Repeated splits change the answer

The study creates 10 replicates for each task and split scheme. A **replicate** is
a new split made with the same rule. The mean describes the centre of the
results. The minimum and maximum show the range across the 10 runs.

Unlike five-fold cross-validation, repeated holdout does not guarantee that each
speech appears in exactly one test set. Here it measures sensitivity to the split
and plays no part in model selection.

```{r}
score_table <- split_summary |>
  transmute(
    task = recode(as.character(task), !!!task_labels),
    split_scheme = as.character(split_scheme),
    mean_accuracy = round(mean_accuracy, 4),
    mean_bal_accuracy = round(mean_bal_accuracy, 4),
    train_majority_accuracy = round(mean_train_majority, 4),
    test_majority_rate = round(mean_test_majority, 4),
    length_rule_accuracy = round(mean_length_rule, 4),
    low_accuracy = round(low_accuracy, 4),
    high_accuracy = round(high_accuracy, 4),
    missing_bal_accuracy = bal_accuracy_missing
  )

get_summary <- function(task_name, scheme_name) {
  split_summary |>
    filter(task == task_name, split_scheme == scheme_name)
}

era_speech <- get_summary("era", "speech")
era_president <- get_summary("era", "president")
era_party_speech <- get_summary("era_party_rows", "speech")
era_party_president <- get_summary("era_party_rows", "president")
party_paragraph <- get_summary("party", "paragraph")
party_speech <- get_summary("party", "speech")
party_president <- get_summary("party", "president")

na_replicate <- study |>
  filter(task == "era_party_rows", split_scheme == "president", is.na(bal_accuracy))

era_speech_range_width <- era_speech$high_accuracy - era_speech$low_accuracy

era_speech_length_gap <- era_speech$mean_accuracy - era_speech$mean_length_rule

era_party_speech_gap <- era_party_speech$mean_accuracy - era_party_speech$mean_train_majority

paired_comparisons <- bind_rows(
  study |>
    filter(task == "era", split_scheme == "speech") |>
    summarise(
      comparison = "era, all rows",
      model_wins = sum(accuracy > train_majority_accuracy),
      ties = sum(accuracy == train_majority_accuracy),
      model_losses = sum(accuracy < train_majority_accuracy)
    ),
  study |>
    filter(task == "era_party_rows", split_scheme == "speech") |>
    summarise(
      comparison = "era, party rows",
      model_wins = sum(accuracy > train_majority_accuracy),
      ties = sum(accuracy == train_majority_accuracy),
      model_losses = sum(accuracy < train_majority_accuracy)
    ),
  study |>
    filter(task == "party", split_scheme == "paragraph") |>
    summarise(
      comparison = "party, paragraph split",
      model_wins = sum(accuracy > train_majority_accuracy),
      ties = sum(accuracy == train_majority_accuracy),
      model_losses = sum(accuracy < train_majority_accuracy)
    )
)

party_president_bal_range <- range(
  study$bal_accuracy[
    study$task == "party" &
      study$split_scheme == "president"
  ]
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

  col.names = c(
    "Task", "Split", "Model accuracy", "Balanced accuracy",
    "Training-majority rule", "Test-majority rate", "Length rule",
    "Model low", "Model high", "Missing balanced accuracy"
  ),
  caption = "Ten split replicates for each task and split scheme",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(

  col.names = c("Comparison", "Higher model accuracy", "Equal accuracy", "Lower model accuracy"),
  caption = "Paired model-versus-training-majority results across 10 replicates",

)
```

The speech split is the main era test. The model averages
`r round(era_speech$mean_accuracy, 4)`, while the deployable majority rule
averages `r round(era_speech$mean_train_majority, 4)` and the paragraph-length
rule averages `r round(era_speech$mean_length_rule, 4)`. The model's lowest
speech-split replicate is `r round(era_speech$low_accuracy, 4)`, which is still
higher than the best mean reached by either simple rule. Across the 10 speech
replicates, the model ranges from `r round(era_speech$low_accuracy, 4)` to
`r round(era_speech$high_accuracy, 4)`. The deployable rule ranges from
`r round(era_speech$low_train_majority, 4)` to
`r round(era_speech$high_train_majority, 4)`, and the length rule ranges from
`r round(era_speech$low_length_rule, 4)` to
`r round(era_speech$high_length_rule, 4)`.

Compare a model with the strongest simple alternative evaluated. Here paragraph
length is associated with era, so a length-only rule provides an important
comparison. The model's mean speech-split accuracy exceeds that rule by about
`r round(100 * era_speech_length_gap, 1)` points. The text features therefore
contribute beyond paragraph length alone.

```{r}
#| label: fig-split-study
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy over 10 replicates for the model and low-cost rules."
#| fig-alt: "A dot-and-line chart has two panels: one for the era task and one for the party task. In the era panel, model accuracy is above both the training-majority rule and the paragraph-length rule for all three split schemes: paragraph, speech, and president. The party panel shows model accuracy near or below the training-majority rule for all three split schemes."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"

source("R/lesson-figures.R")

plot_data <- study |>
  filter(task %in% c("era", "party")) |>
  mutate(
    task = recode(task, !!!task_labels),
    split_scheme = factor(split_scheme, levels = split_levels)
  ) |>
  select(task, split_scheme, replicate, accuracy, train_majority_accuracy, length_rule_accuracy) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(accuracy, train_majority_accuracy, length_rule_accuracy),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "score"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = recode(
      measure,
      accuracy = "model",
      train_majority_accuracy = "training-majority rule",
      length_rule_accuracy = "paragraph-length rule"
    )
  )

mean_scores <- plot_data |>
  summarise(score = mean(score), .by = c(task, split_scheme, measure))

measure_colours <- c(
  "model" = lesson_colours[["accent"]],
  "training-majority rule" = lesson_colours[["contrast"]],
  "paragraph-length rule" = lesson_colours[["support"]]
)
measure_label_colours <- c(
  "model" = lesson_text_colours[["accent"]],
  "training-majority rule" = lesson_text_colours[["contrast"]],
  "paragraph-length rule" = lesson_text_colours[["support"]]
)

# The y scale is left to the data. Fixing the lower bound at 0.3 would drop the
# two replicates where the training-majority rule scores 0.27, and those
# are exactly the cases worth seeing: the rule collapses when the class that was
# largest in training is the smaller one in test.
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = split_scheme, y = score, colour = measure)) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.35,
    size = 1.5,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 4401)
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = mean_scores,
    aes(group = measure, linetype = measure),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_point(data = mean_scores, size = 2.6) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = mean_scores |>
      filter(split_scheme == last(split_levels)),
    aes(label = measure, colour = I(measure_label_colours[measure])),
    direction = "y",
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.3,
    segment.colour = NA,
    family = lesson_font,
    size = 3.4,
    seed = 4402
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(task)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = measure_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "model" = "solid",
      "training-majority rule" = "22",
      "paragraph-length rule" = "42"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.3, 2.1))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "Era accuracy is higher for the model than for both rules. The party comparison is less clear.",
    subtitle = "Accuracy in 10 replicates per split scheme. Lines join the replicate means.",
    x = "Split scheme",
    y = "Accuracy"
  ) +
  theme_lesson(grid = "y")
```

```{r}
#| include: false

era_means <- mean_scores |>
  filter(task == task_labels[["era"]]) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = score)
party_means <- mean_scores |>
  filter(task == task_labels[["party"]]) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = score)

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(plot_data), 180L),
  identical(
    plot_data |>

      pull(n),
    rep(10L, 18L)
  ),
  all(plot_data$score >= 0 & plot_data$score <= 1),
  identical(round(min(plot_data$score), 4), 0.2749),
  identical(nrow(mean_scores), 18L),
  all(era_means$model > era_means$`training-majority rule`),
  all(era_means$model > era_means$`paragraph-length rule`),
```

At the paragraph split, the party model does not perform better than its deployable majority rule on average.
The mean is `r round(party_paragraph$mean_accuracy, 4)` for the model against
`r round(party_paragraph$mean_train_majority, 4)` for the rule. Across
the 10 paired replicates, model accuracy is higher in 3, equal in 1, and lower in 6. At the speech
split, the model averages `r round(party_speech$mean_accuracy, 4)` against
`r round(party_speech$mean_train_majority, 4)`.

Under the person split, accuracy
is `r round(party_president$mean_accuracy, 4)` and mean balanced accuracy is
`r round(party_president$mean_bal_accuracy, 4)`. The replicate balanced-accuracy values range from
`r round(party_president_bal_range[[1]], 4)` to
`r round(party_president_bal_range[[2]], 4)`. That range includes values below and above the theoretical
two-class chance value of 0.5. The conclusion concerns this model: this penalty,
recipe, and row set did not consistently predict party correctly.

## The controlled comparison is smaller

The era and party tasks are not a clean pair by default. Party keeps only the
Democratic and Republican speeches, which leaves
`r baseline_display$rows[baseline_display$task == "party"]` of the full
`r baseline_display$rows[baseline_display$task == "era"]` paragraphs. The dropped
rows are from other party labels, and those rows are concentrated in the earliest
speeches with longer paragraphs.

The controlled comparison is `era_party_rows`, which uses the era label on the
same rows as the party model. On the full era corpus, model accuracy is higher than the
deployable rule's accuracy in all 10 speech-level replicates. On the party-row subset, the
model averages `r round(era_party_speech$mean_accuracy, 4)` against
`r round(era_party_speech$mean_train_majority, 4)` for the training-majority
rule. Model accuracy is higher in 6 paired replicates and lower in 4. The mean gap is only
`r round(100 * era_party_speech_gap, 1)` points because this subset is much more
imbalanced, and its direction is not stable across splits.

The full-row results provide evidence for era prediction by this model. The model does not
consistently predict party correctly. The controlled subset provides weaker
evidence for era prediction.

For `era_party_rows` under the person split, replicate
`r na_replicate$replicate[[1]]` has undefined balanced accuracy because the test
set has only one class. Its test-majority rate is
`r round(na_replicate$test_majority_rate[[1]], 4)`, so the accuracy for that one
replicate is not a two-class result. The summary table uses `na.rm = TRUE` for
balanced accuracy and reports the missing count so the case stays visible.

## Read the final confusion matrix

**Sensitivity** is the share of `before 1900` paragraphs assigned to that first
factor level. **Specificity** is the share of `1900 or later` paragraphs assigned
to the second level. Naming the event level matters because reversing the factor
levels reverses which class each measure describes.

```{r}
source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")
paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()

set.seed(4301)
era_split <- group_initial_split(paragraphs, group = speech_id, prop = 0.75)
era_training <- training(era_split)
era_testing <- testing(era_split)

era_recipe <- recipe(era ~ paragraph, data = era_training) |>
  step_tokenize(paragraph) |>
  step_stopwords(paragraph) |>
  step_tokenfilter(paragraph, max_tokens = 500) |>
  step_tfidf(paragraph)

era_model <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 0) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

era_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(era_recipe) |>
  add_model(era_model)

set.seed(4302)
era_fitted <- fit(era_workflow, data = era_training)

era_predictions <- predict(era_fitted, era_testing) |>
  bind_cols(era_testing |> select(era))

final_training_majority <- era_training |>
  count(era, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(era)
final_split_baseline <- mean(era_testing$era == final_training_majority)

confusion <- conf_mat(
  era_predictions,
  truth = era,
  estimate = .pred_class
)
confusion_table <- as.data.frame(confusion$table) |>
  as_tibble()

metric_table <- metric_set(accuracy, bal_accuracy, sens, spec)(
  era_predictions,
  truth = era,
  estimate = .pred_class
) |>
  select(.metric, .estimate) |>
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      .metric = "training_majority_accuracy",
      .estimate = final_split_baseline
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  confusion_table,
  col.names = c("Prediction", "Reference label", "Paragraphs"),
  caption = "Confusion matrix for one speech-held-out era model",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  metric_table |>
    mutate(.estimate = round(.estimate, 4)),
  col.names = c("Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "Model measures and the same-split deployable baseline",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(era_testing), 335L),
  identical(as.character(final_training_majority), "1900 or later"),
  identical(round(final_split_baseline, 4), 0.4179),
  identical(confusion_table$Freq, c(145, 50, 10, 130)),
  identical(
    round(metric_table$.estimate, 4),
    c(0.8209, 0.8361, 0.7436, 0.9286, 0.4179)
  )
)
```

The model gives correct labels to `r confusion_table$Freq[[1]]` early-era paragraphs and
misses `r confusion_table$Freq[[2]]` of them. It gives correct labels to
`r confusion_table$Freq[[4]]` later-era paragraphs and misses
`r confusion_table$Freq[[3]]` of them. Balanced accuracy is
`r round(metric_table$.estimate[metric_table$.metric == "bal_accuracy"], 4)`,
which gives both classes equal weight. The model accuracy is
`r round(metric_table$.estimate[metric_table$.metric == "accuracy"], 4)`.
The deployable training-majority rule scores
`r round(final_split_baseline, 4)` on these same rows.

## What else could produce this score

Era is a deterministic function of `year`, and `year` is constant within a
speech. The era study has `r baseline_display$speeches[baseline_display$task == "era"]`
independent speech units, not `r baseline_display$rows[baseline_display$task == "era"]`
independent paragraphs. The speech split averages about
`r round(era_speech$mean_test_speeches, 1)` speeches per test set. That is why the
model range across speech splits is `r round(era_speech_range_width, 4)`, not the
tighter range one might expect from hundreds of independent rows. The 10
replicates describe resampling variability within one corpus. They do not
provide a confidence interval for political speech outside this collection.

The next lesson prints this model's largest coefficients. The earlier-era
terms mainly reflect formal register, the vocabulary of a particular style of
nineteenth-century public address. They do not necessarily indicate subject
matter.

Terms associated with the later era include `industrial`, `economic`,
`international`, and `federal`. Those terms more directly reflect differences
in subject matter. The score therefore combines style and subject information,
but this analysis does not separate their contributions. Transcription and
typesetting conventions can also differ between nineteenth- and
twenty-first-century texts. This page does not distinguish those effects from
style or subject.

The lesson provides evidence for the limited claim that this text permits era
prediction. It does not establish that the model learned what a period was
about. Separating period vocabulary from register requires further analysis,
such as a stylometric model or a paragraph-length-matched subsample.

## When a model grades another model

Generated text rarely has one correct answer, so many projects use a language
model to score other outputs. Large comparisons find strong agreement with
people on some tasks and weak agreement on others. Judges can also favour
answers because of their position in the prompt or their length.

Before using judge scores, compare them with human ratings on a random sample
from your task. Reverse the order of the answers in comparisons. Report
agreement with a chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa. The guide
[Using a language model in a reproducible analysis](../using-language-models.qmd)
shows the same pattern of checks for model labels.

## What to remember

- A score with no baseline is hard to interpret.
- Candidate selection must finish before the final test set is opened.
- Group splits need same-split baselines, not only corpus-wide baselines.
- One split gives one number. Repeated splits show the range.
- The score's meaning depends on the split scheme.
- This text model learned era well. This penalty and feature set did not
  consistently predict party correctly. That does not establish that party
  prediction is impossible.
- A language model used as a judge needs the same checks against people.

A useful evaluation states which predictions agree with reference labels and
where the evidence stops.
